# Execution Harnesses and Tool Isolation {#sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces}

::: {.epigraph}
> "We shape our tools and thereafter they shape us."
>
> — John M. Culkin, "A Schoolman's Guide to Marshall McLuhan" [@Culkin1967Schoolman, p. 70]
:::

::: {.callout-crux}
**Governing question:** *What is an architecture design environment, and what must it provide for AI-native work?*

**Core thesis:** *An environment is not a simulator wrapper; it coordinates state, tools, workloads, interfaces, failure handling, and multi-fidelity execution to enable closed-loop automated design.*
:::

A tool command is not an environment. An architect can launch a simulator, compiler, formal engine, or physical-design flow and still be unable to say which candidate ran, which state the tool inherited, what an unfamiliar warning meant, or whether a retry repeated the same work. Generative models and automated optimizers widen that gap because they can propose candidates far faster than tools can evaluate them. Once admitted, each evaluation must remain tied to the intended design while sharing licenses, storage, and compute with other work.

Wrappers, harnesses, and isolated sandboxes assemble an execution environment that preserves this connection (@fig-ch06-cover-map). Setup defines the permitted design changes, fixes shared study inputs, and establishes typed tool interfaces and the history linking inputs to derived artifacts. At runtime, the harness carries those definitions into concurrent execution, isolating each attempt and controlling access to shared resources. Recovery and reuse must preserve the same discipline, so a retry remains linked to its failed predecessor and a cached artifact is reused only when it suits the requested operation. The resulting execution records bind returned observations to the inputs, tool versions, and operating conditions that produced them while retaining the cost of every attempt.

These records also preserve the limits of what executed. In the prospective Lighthouse mobile extended-reality (XR) system-on-chip (SoC) study, a retained CACTI run of the analytical static random-access memory (SRAM) model returns values for a 22\ nm process rather than the 3\ nm-class target. Because the intended target comparison and its downstream simulation and physical-implementation steps have not been run, recording what ran and what returned makes those limits inspectable, while deciding what the observations prove about the architecture requires the verification discipline in @sec-feedback-verification-trust.

![**Nested boundaries turn authorized requests into complete execution records for later qualification.** The environment separates tool wrappers, execution harnesses, and outer sandboxes so that each run isolates tool state, records compute and license costs, and logs the metadata needed to audit simulation and synthesis outputs before they drive the next design step. The diagram is schematic and carries no measured values.](images/ch06-cover-map.svg){#fig-ch06-cover-map width="100%" fig-alt="Chapter overview diagram in which nested environment, harness, wrapper, and tool boundaries turn an authorized request into a complete execution record for later qualification."}

## Architecture of the Tool Execution Harness

Consider one evaluation in the cache-capacity comparison introduced in @sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization. The caller requests a candidate and workload, and the environment translates that request into simulator inputs, allocates resources, and launches the tool. After execution, it returns cycle counts and miss rates alongside the run status, logs, and resource cost. The same interface can serve a direct comparison of supplied candidates or an optimizer choosing its next candidate from earlier results.

Now consider what happens when a twelve-hour full-system simulation fails at hour eight from an out-of-memory kernel kill and a naive script immediately relaunches the command. Before trusting the new result, the architect has to answer three operational questions. Did the restart resume from a clean memory checkpoint or start over from cold reset? Did it inherit modified host environment variables or leftover scratch files from the failed attempt? Did the accounting log charge the compute time already consumed against the study's budget? Because a bare shell retry discards that failure context, later comparisons can silently mix a cold start with a resumed run or undercount the true cost of the search.

An execution environment therefore provides both an interface for requesting work and the machinery that carries it out. The interface defines permitted actions and returned information, while the machinery manages processes, workspaces, licenses, and resources. Whereas human engineers handle much of this coordination in an interactive computer-aided design (CAD) flow, an automated loop must perform it in software across concurrent candidates and heterogeneous tools, and keeping the interface separate from the runtime machinery lets a team start with a small harness and expand it as the study grows.

### From Tools to an Execution Environment

Suppose a generative model proposes a revised cache coherence controller in register-transfer level (RTL) code. A single shell script writes its testbench, runs Verilator, parses the log, and launches synthesis in Yosys. When two candidates run concurrently, they can overwrite the same scratch files; when a report format changes, a parsing failure can look like a failed assertion. Separating the executable from its adapter and coordinator makes these failures distinguishable:

- **Tool:** The standalone executable that performs a domain-specific transformation or analysis, such as compiling software with LLVM, synthesizing RTL code into gates with Yosys, or evaluating physical timing with OpenSTA. It consumes files in proprietary or standard formats and emits log reports or physical artifacts.
- **Simulator:** A specialized class of tool that models hardware or software behavior over time. For example, gem5 executes an event-driven, cycle-level microarchitectural model, yielding cycle counts, cache hit distributions, and bus contention statistics under configured workload assumptions.
- **Wrapper:** The adapter that bridges an individual tool to the environment's typed contract. It validates request parameters, generates tool-specific command scripts and configuration files, manages process invocation, parses unstructured text logs into strongly typed metrics, and flags syntax or runtime errors.
- **Harness:** The workflow coordinator that runs multi-tool execution pipelines. It resolves candidate dependency graphs, manages concurrent dispatch, arbitrates shared resources such as license tokens and GPU queues, handles timeouts and retries, and binds execution outcomes to parent artifacts.
- **Environment:** The overarching system that encapsulates the design state, permitted action space, tool interfaces, and security sandboxes. It governs what the search method can observe, modify, and evaluate, establishing the boundary between the search method and tool execution.

On that coherence-controller check, each layer handles a separate piece of the job. The wrapper generates the testbench driver, launches Verilator inside an isolated scratch directory, and extracts assertion outcomes. The harness tracks the run, logs its memory and CPU consumption, and triggers downstream gate-level synthesis through Yosys only after the functional check passes. Surrounding both, the environment dictates whether the generator may modify arbitrary state machines, tune clock periods in a Synopsys Design Constraints (SDC) file, or merely sweep buffer capacities within a fixed netlist.

The operational scope defined in @sec-three-operational-layers changes what this machinery must accept. While an engineer can coordinate the tool work for an isolated generated snippet by hand, an automated parameter search needs a repeatable path from supported settings to tool inputs, and a system that proposes organizations beyond the existing template must also accept new artifacts and update their dependencies. In each case, the required checks follow the design claim, so a fast model can guide exploration within the range where it was validated against a slower reference tool while an implementation-facing claim still requires the relevant physical checks.

Existing electronic design automation (EDA) frameworks already provide many of the adapters such a multi-tool flow needs. SiliconCompiler connects design data, tool settings, and process design kit (PDK) information through a shared schema and execution flow [@SiliconCompiler]. Hammer separates tool-specific steps, technology information, and project configuration behind plugin interfaces [@Hammer]. These frameworks handle the mechanics of invoking hardware tools, but the study still has to define which actions its methods can request, how returned results re-enter the design loop, and how shared cluster resources are protected when many evaluations run concurrently.

### Tool Requests, Wrappers, and Returns

Driving a tool through raw command strings leaves simple mistakes undetected until late in execution. A clock period expressed in picoseconds may be read as nanoseconds, or a misspelled library path may trigger a default after the job has waited for a license. A typed interface makes the requested action explicit before dispatch. It distinguishes a source-artifact handle, a clock period with units, and a wall-clock timeout even if the tool eventually receives all three as text. Field types catch structural mistakes; domain preconditions check whether the library and design state are suitable for the requested analysis.

For the coherence controller example, an environment might expose separate actions to submit an RTL implementation, synthesize an identified version, and evaluate its timing. A synthesis request identifies the source artifact, top-level module, target library, and clock constraints, while its return identifies any generated netlist and log reports alongside execution and parsing status. If the study holds the technology library fixed, the interface resolves that library from the study configuration and rejects requests that try to override it. An interface that accepts arbitrary module implementations lets a generator revise the controller anywhere within the study's scope. One limited to predefined scalar parameters confines the search to the knobs on that list.

Whether an action submits a full module or adjusts scalar knobs, tool interfaces can share submission, cancellation, status, cost, and artifact-reference fields while retaining tool-specific inputs and outputs. Because synthesis with Yosys and physical layout with OpenROAD consume different files and constraints [@Yosys; @AjayiEtAl2019OpenROAD], and a timing slack in picoseconds and a simulator's instructions per cycle (IPC) measure different properties even when both return as numbers, the shared interface must preserve those distinctions.

When those tool-specific inputs modify hardware structure rather than scalar parameters, a structured intermediate representation (IR) makes the allowed transformation easier to express and check than raw text substitution. The Circuit IR Compilers and Tools (CIRCT) hardware dialects built on Multi-Level Intermediate Representation (MLIR), introduced in @sec-data-representations-world-models [@LattnerEtAl2020MLIR; @CIRCT], let the interface reject structurally invalid edits by running the IR and dialect verifiers before accepting them. Downstream simulation or formal checks are still required because structural validity does not prove that the revised circuit meets its functional specification.

Once a request clears those interface checks, a wrapper translates the typed request into the individual tool's inputs. For the controller synthesis request, it resolves the specified RTL and library, writes the clock constraints, and prepares the command. If the backend cannot express a required setting, the wrapper reports the limitation or refuses the request rather than substituting a default that changes the design question. Before launch, the wrapper also checks required fields, allowed parameter ranges, and availability of the identified files. Passing those checks shows that the request can proceed, not that the hardware is correct or the tool will finish.

The return path needs the same care. Once execution yields a process exit code, log reports, and physical artifacts, a dedicated parser extracts typed metrics, units, and operating conditions and keeps the raw logs for audit. The interface flow in @fig-environment-tool-interface binds these outputs to the originating request and records the compute and license resources consumed. A translation error or an unparseable log then cannot masquerade as a design result.

![**Tool wrappers separate process execution from log parsing.** Invalid requests bypass the tool and go straight to the execution record; completed, partial, or failed runs pass their raw files to a parser that extracts typed metrics, flags parse errors, and retains unrecognized output alongside runtime cost and lineage. The diagram is schematic and carries no measured values.](images/fig-environment-tool-interface.svg){#fig-environment-tool-interface width="80%" fig-alt="Flow diagram in which an architecture question and workload, action schema, constraints, and metric definitions enter the tool-connected environment as a typed request. The wrapper validates and translates the request before calling the tool. An invalid request goes directly to the harness record. The tool separately produces raw returned material and a runtime outcome that can be failed, partial, or complete. The parser turns retained raw material into structured attributes, unclassified residual output, and a parse status. The harness records request and attempt identity, conditions, runtime outcome, artifacts, parse status, cost, and lineage."}

As @fig-environment-tool-interface shows, an invalid request goes directly to a refused execution record without launching the tool. For an admitted request, runtime outcome and parsing status remain independent: a crashed simulation differs from a completed run whose report the parser cannot read. Missing metrics stay distinct from measured zeros. Raw reports and unrecognized lines remain available so a reviewer can inspect warnings or missing-clock messages that a scalar summary would hide.

Before relying on a wrapper, the team tests sample requests against expected tool inputs and representative logs against expected returns. Unit conversion, unsupported settings, and missing outputs need checks alongside successful runs. Fault injection, a distributed-systems testing practice [@GunawiEtAl2011FATEDestini], tests whether timeouts, killed processes, and truncated logs produce the promised status and retained diagnostics. Correct translation and parsing still leave one hidden input to control: the state inherited by the tool process.

### Managing Stateful Tools and Cross-Stage Translation

A tool's starting state is part of its input, even when the request does not name it. A physical-design session may hold an in-memory netlist and placement database, or a simulator may resume from a checkpoint; OpenROAD, for example, can save and reload its design database [@OpenROADDocs]. If revised controller RTL is evaluated using a database built for the previous candidate, the report describes the old design under the new candidate's name. Leftover floorplans, extracted wire parasitics, or timing graphs in a shared workspace can cause the same mismatch.

The simplest way to prevent inherited state is to launch a fresh process in an empty workspace with a clean environment-variable table, provided the wrapper loads the intended inputs and settings. When a study reuses a live session or checkpoint to avoid repeated startup cost, the harness must make that reuse explicit and checkable. A reset must restore the required baseline state, and a deliberate continuation must record the exact checkpoint, in-memory database, and temporary files it builds on.

State consistency also matters between tools. Yosys can synthesize RTL into a gate-level netlist mapped to a target cell library [@Yosys]; a physical flow such as OpenROAD pairs that netlist with the corresponding timing and physical library views [@OpenROADDocs]. Liberty (`.lib`) files, Library Exchange Format (LEF) files, and Unified Power Format (UPF) power intent supply different parts of that context [@Synopsys2012LibertyFormat; @Si2LEFDEF; @IEEE2024UPF].[^fn-eda-formats-c06] The environment must keep these views compatible as the candidate changes.

[^fn-eda-formats-c06]: **EDA library and power-intent formats**: In a standard-cell flow, `.lib` tables characterize delay and energy per pin transition across operating corners, LEF abstracts expose macro geometry and pin layers to the placer and router without disclosing internal transistor layouts, and UPF specifies voltage domains, level shifters, and retention registers without supplying a power model of its own.

Collecting these files under one candidate identifier does not guarantee that they still agree. Suppose a generator widens a block's interface but leaves an older LEF physical abstract in place, or modifies power domains without updating the UPF power intent. Or suppose timing analysis uses `.lib` delays characterized at a 0.75\ V process, voltage, and temperature (PVT) corner when the request specifies another voltage. In each case, the returned timing and power describe a mismatched design or operating condition. The environment must therefore track which inputs each tool path depends on and verify their compatibility before admitting the results.

Translation into tool-specific syntax carries a related obligation. A wrapper may convert units or reformat settings, and different tools may legitimately model a candidate at different levels of abstraction, provided the modeled properties and their limits stay explicit. Silently rounding a buffer capacity or changing an array dimension, however, creates a different candidate. When a backend cannot represent a required feature, the design loop should choose another evaluation path, because changing the candidate just to make a tool run succeed is a new design proposal rather than a translation repair.

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Preserve the requested design across every tool boundary"}
**The principle:** A wrapper translates a request into a tool's syntax without changing the candidate, its operating conditions, or its starting state; when it cannot, it refuses the request or reports the limitation.

**The application:** A run that used a default clock, a different library view, a rounded capacity, or state inherited from an earlier attempt still carries the requested candidate's identity while describing a different design. Check translation, starting state, and input compatibility before launch, and give any change made only to get a run through its own identity as a new proposal.
:::

The prospective Lighthouse study illustrates what this translation discipline requires when a single SoC proposal must reach analytical, cycle-level, and RTL tools.

::: {.callout-lighthouse title="One XR SoC request, several tool representations"}
**Context.** The tool paths would need different inputs to represent the same Lighthouse candidate.

**Application.** Consider a candidate with a 3\ MiB cache, a neural processing unit (NPU) array ($16 \times 16$), and dual LPDDR5 channels. An analytical model would use the dimensions and PVT assumptions relevant to its estimates. A configured gem5 model would represent the supported timing behavior, while a Verilator-based path would execute the supplied RTL and testbench. Each path would need matching workload inputs or traffic generators and an explicit account of which candidate features it represents.

**Required behavior.** Across these paths, wrappers must preserve relevant capacities, dimensions, cache policies, and memory arbitration wherever those properties are modeled, and report any unsupported feature rather than silently replacing it with a default. Because these rules specify requirements for the unexecuted study rather than observed wrapper results, any differences between tool outputs must be interpreted in light of each path's model assumptions and operating conditions.
:::

### Host and Network Boundaries

The tool path runs on hosts with finite compute, shared storage, and access to project data. Commercial EDA tools also require license checkouts, often managed by a server such as FlexLM.[^fn-flexlm-c06] Adding workers cannot increase throughput once the required seats are exhausted. The harness must account for those shared resources when admitting work, while preserving the host conditions needed to interpret runtime measurements. CPU frequency, memory locality, and competing storage traffic can alter elapsed time without changing the modeled design; @sec-incremental-churn-dispersion separates this host variation from changes in returned design metrics.

Beyond managing shared host resources, the harness must restrict what generated scripts can access on the host and network. Tcl can launch shell commands with the tool process's permissions, so a synthesis script may otherwise overwrite unrelated files or send data over the network. An isolated environment grants each run only the writable paths, libraries, and connections it requires. Unprivileged containers, read-only library mounts, and network restrictions can enforce parts of that boundary, but a container with broad host access provides little containment.

Confidential data needs a boundary of its own. When an external model proposes changes against internal foundry collateral, the limits on what may be disclosed must cover returned reports and retrieved context as well as input files. Removing absolute delays or layout coordinates from a report does not by itself establish that the remaining information may be disclosed.

Even when every file stays on internal hosts, physical-design runs produce large databases and checkpoints. Concurrent writes can saturate shared storage, so a harness may use node-local scratch space and move needed outputs to persistent storage before releasing it. Retention follows the next use: a parser repair needs raw reports, a resumed run needs a checkpoint, and review may need implementation artifacts beyond scalar metrics. Failed candidates still need the material required for diagnosis; bulky intermediates can be discarded once their uses end, with the execution record stating what remains available.

These controls isolate individual runs. Keeping results comparable across a changing project additionally requires fixing the inputs and recording the dependencies that each run used.

[^fn-flexlm-c06]: **License checkout**: A tool requests access to a licensed feature before using it. Depending on the tool's integration with the license manager, unavailable capacity may cause the request to wait or fail; the harness must distinguish that outcome from an analysis that ran and found a design problem.

## Preserving Inputs Across Tool Paths

A correct wrapper can still evaluate the wrong comparison if its inputs live in mutable project directories. During a multi-day search, an edit to a shared constraint file or compiler script can change the baseline for subsequent candidates. Setup therefore fixes the shared study inputs while allowing new candidate artifacts to be registered as the loop proceeds. Each submitted candidate must remain tied to the library views, constraints, workload, and tool configuration used for its evaluation.

The resulting history must survive further design changes. A new controller revision should add a branch to that history, not overwrite the source or netlist that produced an earlier report. Preserving those relationships requires lineage across the tool paths.

### Lineage and Reproducibility

In a conventional project layout, tools write compiled binaries, elaborated RTL, and synthesized netlists into a single mutable `build/` directory. Once an automated loop branches across dozens of candidates and retries failed runs out of order, in-place builds break down. A late retry overwrites an earlier candidate's synthesis output, or a revised RTL module runs timing analysis against a stale netlist from the previous iteration. To know which existing artifacts still apply and which must be regenerated, the environment needs an explicit dependency graph and recorded *lineage*: the history linking requests, transformations, and artifacts. Lineage shows which inputs produced an output, which candidate version an evaluation actually used, and how a retry relates to an earlier attempt. To keep that history intact, the environment stores immutable snapshots of source files, constraints, and library views apart from mutable working directories, so later edits never overwrite what an earlier run used.

A lineage entry links an output to its parent artifacts, the tool and settings that produced it, its operating conditions, and the checks it has passed. Content hashes identify the retained file contents; the dependency links explain how they were used. When an optimizer changes a parameter in a high-level C++ hardware model, derived RTL and gate netlists must be regenerated or shown to remain applicable. A testbench may remain usable if its stimulus and reference checks are independent of the change, but not when the parameter determines its expected outputs. Selective rebuilding therefore depends on recording every input that influences the transformation.

In @fig-artifact-lineage, a single architectural intent branches through software compilation and hardware elaboration, then rejoins in an evaluation key that identifies the combined software and hardware inputs. A later search iteration can branch off these existing artifacts without overwriting the lineage of earlier evaluations.

![**Evaluated software and hardware artifacts retain explicit parent transformation lineage.** An architectural intent branches into parallel software compilation (MLIR to binary) and hardware elaboration (Chisel to RTL) paths, where each intermediate artifact inherits parent hashes, tool versions, and operating conditions before joining into a composite evaluation key. The diagram is schematic; its hash labels are placeholders, not recorded digests.](images/fig-artifact-lineage.svg){#fig-artifact-lineage width="80%" fig-alt="Lineage diagram in which a single Lighthouse intent branches into a software variant and a hardware variant. The software compiles into an identified binary, and the hardware elaborates into an identified RTL artifact. An evaluation instance binds both artifacts to the tool and version, workload, and operating conditions. Hashes and evaluation keys distinguish exact artifacts and paths but do not prove functional equivalence or reproducibility."}

To identify the exact combination under test, the environment constructs an evaluation key from all declared inputs that distinguish one evaluation from another, including content hashes of the design artifacts and workload, tool and container versions, and relevant command settings. Upgrading a compiler version therefore produces a new evaluation key even if the output binary happens to be unchanged. Repeated executions of the same evaluation key still receive separate execution records, so their individual outcomes and compute costs remain distinct.

Operating conditions belong in this history as well. In physical timing analysis, a slack of -12\ ps (the path's data arrives 12\ ps after its clock deadline) at a slow corner and the same slack at a typical corner describe different physical regimes. The two numbers can be compared only when their corner conditions stay attached to them. Software and simulator measurements are similarly sensitive to environmental details outside the source program: experiments have shown that changing nothing more than Unix link order or the size of the shell environment can shift code and stack alignment enough to bias performance comparisons [@Mytkowicz2009WrongData]. The practical defense is to record every execution condition that can affect the property being measured.

### Tool Paths and Fidelity

A revised controller raises several questions: does it behave correctly, how does it affect workload execution, and can its implementation meet timing? Different tools address different parts of that evaluation. The execution environment binds the design representations of @sec-data-representations-world-models into runnable tool paths, each with its own required inputs, simplifying assumptions, and outputs.

Fidelity is relative to the property under study (@sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization); for the environment, changing fidelity means changing tool paths. @tbl-observation-source-limits recorded what each observation source sees and misses; the environment's added job is to preserve, for every tool path, the state that later work needs to interpret its return. An RTL simulation exposes cycle-by-cycle protocol behavior that an analytical model omits, static timing analysis computes gate and wire delays that an unannotated RTL simulation ignores, and a formal check proves stated invariants under its declared assumptions. Greater detail in one of these evaluations cannot replace missing coverage in the others.

Because these tool classes need not run as one linear pipeline that every candidate traverses (@tbl-multi-fidelity-spectrum), a study can stage its evaluations economically. The harness can run independent checks in parallel and use fast models to screen candidates before launching expensive evaluations, whenever the fast screen has been validated for the property and operating range in question.

The environment must make both the stages and their limits explicit. A calibrated cycle-level model may suffice for a bounded performance comparison, but it cannot establish that a changed organization will route or meet its clock target. If the study needs those properties, its execution path must include the corresponding implementation checks and their inputs. Cheap screening changes which candidates reach those checks; it does not remove the checks from the claim.

| **Tool class** | **Representative use** | **What it models or checks** | **Preserved environment state** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Analytical / circuit model | CACTI, spreadsheet models [@MuralimanoharEtAl2009CACTI]. | Analytical equations and technology assumptions without workload execution. | Model version, macro geometry, PVT conditions, technology limits. |
| Compiler and build stack | TVM, IREE, LLVM pass pipelines, linkers. | Generation of executable binaries; no hardware timing. | Source intermediate representations (IRs), target instruction set architecture (ISA) flags, compiler versions, binary hashes. |
| Functional ISA emulator | Spike, QEMU ISA execution. | Instruction semantics without microarchitectural timing. | Target binary, ISA extensions, input state, functional output. |
| Timing simulation | gem5 [@BinkertEtAl2011Gem5], SST, Ramulator 2, SCALE-Sim. | Pipeline, cache, network-on-chip (NoC), memory controller, and accelerator timing. | Workload inputs, traces, warmup length, seeds, event traces. |
| RTL simulation / testbench | Verilator [@Veripool2026Verilator], cocotb, Synopsys VCS. | Cycle behavior under RTL semantics; no routed delay unless annotated. | RTL hash, testbench, compile flags, waveform traces. |
| Formal verification | SystemVerilog Assertions (SVA) and bounded model checking (BMC) via SymbiYosys or JasperGold [@Clarke2018ModelChecking]. | Stated invariants/relations under declared proof methods and bounds. | Property definitions, assumptions, bounds, solver engine, available proof or counterexample records. |
| Emulation and field-programmable gate array (FPGA) | ZeBu, Palladium, FireSim on cloud FPGAs [@KarandikarEtAl2018FireSim]. | Accelerated target execution. FPGA mapping is not application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC) signoff. | Target bitstream, host allocation, workload snapshot, traces. |
| Physical implementation and signoff | OpenROAD flow; OpenSTA timing; KLayout / Calibre [@OpenROADDocs]. | Placement, routing, timing, design rule checking (DRC), and layout versus schematic (LVS) verification. | Netlist, library/PDK views, SDC constraints, layout and parasitic artifacts, operating corners, stage settings, rule decks. |
: **Each tool path must preserve the state that gives its return meaning.** Fidelity is relative to the property under evaluation, so harnesses preserve model assumptions, inputs, stages, and artifacts rather than collapsing returns into scalar scores. {#tbl-multi-fidelity-spectrum tbl-colwidths="[20,24,28,28]"}

The preserved-state column of @tbl-multi-fidelity-spectrum determines how later work can interpret a return. A formal result needs its property, assumptions, method, and any cycle bound; a completed bounded check cannot establish behavior beyond that bound. A sampled simulation, which measures only selected program intervals using SimPoint or SMARTS, needs its interval-selection method, weights, warmup, and checkpoints [@SherwoodEtAl2002SimPoint; @WunderlichEtAl2003SMARTS]. Without those inputs, the harness would return numbers or statuses while losing the conditions that give them meaning.

A unified design configuration connects these disparate evaluation paths across a project. In an SoC integration framework such as Chipyard [@chipyard], a single root configuration elaborates through Chisel and FIRRTL before branching into software RTL simulation, very-large-scale integration (VLSI) physical implementation, and field-programmable gate array (FPGA)-accelerated execution (@fig-chipyard-framework). Because all three paths start from the same microarchitectural parameters, the study avoids maintaining separate hand-written models for each tool tier. Branch-specific settings and transformations must still be recorded independently. A shared top-level configuration guarantees common starting parameters, but it does not ensure that different backends evaluate identical physical or timing behavior.

![**Unified design configurations anchor multi-tool evaluation flows.** Adapted from the Chipyard SoC framework [@chipyard], one root parameterization feeds Verilator or Synopsys VCS for software RTL simulation, Hammer with OpenROAD or commercial engines for VLSI physical design, and FireSim for FPGA-accelerated execution. Shared lineage keeps parameter changes traceable across tiers without treating their distinct outputs as interchangeable. The diagram is schematic and carries no measured values.](images/fig-chipyard-framework.svg){#fig-chipyard-framework width="80%" fig-alt="Flow diagram in which a common design configuration lowers through Chisel generation and compiler transformations before branching into RTL simulation, VLSI physical implementation, and FPGA-accelerated simulation."}

Shared configuration history traces a result back to its originating candidate, but each output keeps the limits of its own evaluation path. Cycle counts from an unannotated Verilator testbench cannot substitute for post-route timing slack. FPGA execution rates are not application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC) clock frequencies, and FPGA resource usage may reward a design that maps efficiently to lookup tables without establishing its standard-cell area. Using an upstream quantity as a proxy for a downstream property always requires empirical evidence for that relationship. For that reason, the environment keeps the tool identity, model assumptions, operating conditions, and units bound to every metric.

Evaluation throughput is equally tied to what each backend models. For example, ZSim reports about 20\ million instructions per second per simulated core, or roughly a $200\times$ slowdown for its detailed out-of-order model, and its single-thread SPEC CPU2006 evaluation of that model reports harmonic means of 12.4\ million with contention and 14.8\ million without [@ZSim]. The FireSim paper reports a 1,024-node target cluster running on cloud FPGAs at a simulated processor clock rate of 3.4\ MHz, less than $1{,}000\times$ slower than its 3.2\ GHz target [@KarandikarEtAl2018FireSim]. Because simulated target instructions per host second and simulated target cycles per host second count different work against different reference systems, those figures describe distinct modeling regimes rather than a direct speed comparison.

Each execution path therefore reports throughput in its own unit of work (@tbl-ch06-simulation-spectrum). Once a study selects a tool path that observes the required property, the harness can budget evaluation work in those path-specific units. It can also separate the one-time cost of compilation or FPGA bitstream generation from the marginal cost of later workload runs that reuse the built image, which decides whether a faster path that needs more setup pays off for the number of runs planned.

| **Execution path** | **Unit of work or elapsed time** | **Conditions to match** |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Analytical model | Model evaluations / second | Model, candidate size, host |
| ISA execution | Instructions / second | ISA, workload, host |
| Timing / RTL simulation | Target cycles / host second | Target model, workload, host |
| Hardware emulation | Target cycles / host second | Mapped target, workload, testbed |
| Formal verification | Elapsed time / named property | Property, model, bound, solver |
| Physical implementation | Elapsed time / defined stage | Design, libraries, stage settings |
: **Throughput comparisons require a declared unit of work.** Different execution paths count different work: model evaluations, instructions, target cycles, properties, or physical flow stages. The final column identifies conditions needed before even two rates in the same row can be compared. Row order implies no throughput or fidelity ranking. Author-constructed comparison guide, not a measured benchmark. {#tbl-ch06-simulation-spectrum tbl-colwidths="[28,34,38]"}

Existing workflow and environment frameworks provide different parts of this multi-tool integration. ArchGym connects search algorithms to architecture simulators [@KrishnanEtAl2023ArchGym], CHIA supports hardware-software co-design workflows that combine design tools, simulators, software builds, and model calls [@CuiEtAl2026CHIA], and workflow engines such as Nextflow and Snakemake schedule execution dependencies [@DiTommasoEtAl2017Nextflow; @KosterEtAl2012Snakemake]. Whichever framework a team builds on, the study still has to specify which tool path answers each architectural question, which artifacts pass between stages, and what conditions permit reuse. Once those static tool paths, typed interfaces, and lineage rules are configured, the harness must manage their runtime execution as concurrent requests queue, run, and fail on shared cluster hardware.

## Running Parallel Tool Jobs Without Losing State

In an active search campaign, an optimizer regularly proposes a new candidate while an earlier multi-hour gem5 simulation or OpenROAD place-and-route job is still running on the cluster. Without runtime coordination, the new submission can overwrite RTL or constraint files in a live workspace, a batch-scheduler preemption can erase the accounting record of compute time and license hours already spent, and a stalled job can hold a commercial license seat indefinitely.

At runtime, the harness prevents those collisions. It isolates each attempt's working directory, admits requests only as compute slots and EDA licenses open up, tracks active runs across cluster nodes, and binds returned reports, exit statuses, and resource costs to the exact inputs and checkpoints that produced them. An asynchronous interface lets the optimizer submit a candidate and continue exploring while the harness tracks in-flight attempts, contains failures, and decides when completed artifacts can be reused. Supporting that loop starts with submitting and monitoring jobs without accidentally launching duplicate runs.

### Scheduling Parallel Runs and Making Retries Safe

In a synchronous interface, such as the `step()` call in reinforcement learning environments like Gymnasium [@TowersEtAl2023Gymnasium], the call blocks until the action finishes and returns its result directly. Blocking is convenient when an evaluation takes milliseconds, but hardware simulations and physical-design runs can take hours or days. Separating job submission from completion lets a search method submit a candidate, monitor outstanding requests, and continue other work while tools execute through a scheduler adapter connected to Slurm, IBM LSF, or a container service.

Once submission and completion are decoupled, the harness has to distinguish what was requested from how it executes on the cluster. A *request* describes the intended evaluation, an *attempt* records one effort to carry it out, and *backend jobs* perform the actual work across compute nodes. Because a single attempt can map to zero, one, or many backend jobs, the harness keeps its durable execution record separate from those transient cluster processes (@fig-runtime-object-state). Admission may refuse a request outright, dispatch a single simulator process, or fan work across several parallel backend jobs. In every case the outcome reconciles into one execution record, and any subsequent retry creates a new attempt linked explicitly to its predecessor.

![**A single execution record tracks zero, one, or multiple backend tool executions.** An authorized request creates one attempt whose execution record collects returned raw artifacts, realized compute and license costs, and six independent status attributes regardless of whether the request is refused before launch, runs as a single job, or spans multiple cluster segments. The diagram is schematic and carries no measured values.](images/fig-runtime-object-state.svg){#fig-runtime-object-state width="80%" fig-alt="Conceptual state diagram in which an authorized request creates one attempt. The attempt may be refused before a backend job exists, may create one job, or may create several jobs or execution segments. All paths feed one execution record. The execution record points separately to returned artifacts and realized cost. Scheduling state, terminal cause, artifact completeness, parser status, cancellation confirmation, and retry parent remain independent attributes."}

Because an execution record must outlive the processes that perform its work, the harness retains available logs and records the resources already consumed whenever a cluster scheduler preempts a simulation. It tracks six status attributes independently: scheduling state, terminal cause, artifact completeness, parser health, cancellation confirmation, and retry parentage. Keeping these fields separate stops one status from masking another. When a scheduler evicts and requeues a job under the same attempt, each execution segment adds to that attempt's cumulative cost history. When the harness instead launches a fresh recovery attempt, it creates a new execution record linked to its predecessor. Neither path erases the interruption or the consumed core-hours.

Decoupled submission also introduces a classic distributed-systems hazard: the harness accepts a submission, but a network drop or timeout prevents its reply from reaching the caller. To prevent a resent request from launching a second copy of a multi-hour job, submission must be *idempotent*, producing the same system state when repeated [@Featonby2021IdempotentAPIs]. When a caller resubmits the same `submission_token` with the same request contents, the harness returns the existing attempt rather than creating another, and it rejects any call that reuses an old token with modified parameters. Retransmitting a submission whose outcome is unknown is therefore distinct from deliberately retrying failed work, which always uses a fresh token and creates a new, linked attempt.

Making submission genuinely idempotent requires more than checking a token in memory. The harness must record the accepted attempt in durable storage before dispatch and bind the token to the request and its backend jobs. If the harness crashes during dispatch, recovery has to check whether the cluster job already started before launching it again. While that check is underway, `poll` returns `RECONCILING` to indicate that the attempt is registered while its execution state remains uncertain. The caller can continue polling the existing attempt rather than submitting the same work under a new token that would create a duplicate, and recovery must resolve the uncertainty rather than assuming no job started.

The four operations in @lst-harness-interface expose this lifecycle cleanly. Calling `submit` returns an attempt identifier and admission status; `poll` reports progress; and `collect` retrieves the execution record once the attempt reaches a terminal state, including any partial outputs and failures. When several backend jobs belong to an attempt, the harness aggregates their individual states so that one completed job never marks the whole attempt complete prematurely. Finally, `cancel` requests termination, which must be confirmed across all attached work.

```{.yaml #lst-harness-interface lst-cap="**Harness interface shape.** Three normal-path calls submit, poll, and collect an attempt. Polling distinguishes unresolved execution state from known progress or completion. A fourth operation requests cancellation and reports whether termination is confirmed. Refused requests also retain an identifier and a collectable record."}
submit:
  takes: typed request, submission_token
  returns: attempt_id, admission status (ADMITTED | REFUSED)
poll:
  takes: attempt_id
  returns: >-
    REFUSED | QUEUED | RUNNING | EVICTED | RECONCILING |
    COMPLETED | FAILED | CANCELED
collect:
  takes: attempt_id
  returns: execution record (artifacts, parse status, cost, lineage)
cancel:
  takes: attempt_id
  returns: CONFIRMED after all attached work stops | UNCONFIRMED (quarantine)
```

Each state that `poll` reports records what happened to the process, not whether the hardware candidate is valid. A transition to `COMPLETED` indicates only that the underlying operating-system process exited with code zero; it does not guarantee that the tool generated valid metrics or satisfied design constraints. In a static timing engine, a clean exit can occur even when paths with no clock constraint go unchecked and hide real violations, or when false-path waivers, which tell the tool to skip named paths, exclude critical ones. Conversely, an `EVICTED` state means the cluster scheduler preempted the job or reclaimed its node rather than that the candidate failed, so the harness requeues the work while linking the new execution segment to the earlier one. Exploration methods see these attempt-level states, not the individual transitions of each backend job beneath them.

While idempotent submission and attempt-level state tracking prevent duplicate runs, they do not limit the rate of distinct requests. As the capacity analysis in @sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization showed, a fast proposal method can easily overload a slower evaluation stage. The runtime harness enforces that capacity plan through admission limits, bounded queues, and backpressure signals that tell the caller to slow or pause submissions. Even then, free capacity at one stage does not guarantee capacity at the next, because available processors may still be waiting for tool licenses or upstream results.

::: {.callout-law title="Queueing Congestion Collapse in Tool Loops"}
**The Classical Principle:** In a single-server queue with Poisson arrivals and exponential service times, mean time in the system grows without bound as the request arrival rate $\lambda$ approaches the service rate $\mu$ [@Kleinrock1975QueueingSystems]. @sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization extends this capacity bound to a chain of tool stages.

**The Hardware Trap:** A generator proposes candidates faster than the available simulators and licensed tools can evaluate them. Without admission limits, the queue keeps growing, and by the time a simulation finishes, upstream specifications, compiler branches, or interface assumptions may have moved. The result still describes its recorded inputs but may no longer answer the active design question.

**The Architectural Antidote:** Limit admitted work according to downstream capacity, with separate limits for each stage's workers, licenses, and other shared resources. Queue limits reduce the chance that results return after their input assumptions have become stale, but they cannot guarantee freshness when tool durations or upstream changes are unpredictable (@sec-law-congestion-collapse in @sec-appendix-b-laws-paradoxes).
:::

License features can also create deadlock: one job holds a compilation license while waiting for a simulation license, and another holds the simulation license while waiting for compilation. Each holds a resource the other needs [@CoffmanEtAl1971SystemDeadlocks]. Reserving the required features before admission removes that hold-and-wait condition. Once admitted, however, a job can still hang or exhaust its budget, so the harness needs to terminate stalled work and isolate its workspace before recovery.

### Fault Containment and Execution Quarantines

Managing queues and licenses keeps work moving, but the harness also has to clean up safely when a run times out or fails midway. Suppose a synthesis job reaches its wall-clock limit and the harness requests cancellation. If the launcher script exits while a background worker it started is still writing a design database to disk, reusing that workspace for an immediate retry could mix files from the two attempts. Containing a fault requires tracking every process and writable resource belonging to an attempt and verifying whether any of them remain active before recycling the workspace.

Local process controls can track and terminate a tool's workers together.[^fn-process-containment-c06] They do not establish that distributed workers on remote nodes have stopped. The harness must confirm termination through the cluster backend before reclaiming shared resources, while preserving the license and storage access that the tool requires for orderly shutdown.

[^fn-process-containment-c06]: **Process containment**: Commercial EDA tools can spawn background daemons and child processes. If a parent script is killed, live orphaned workers may continue consuming memory and holding licenses. They differ from zombie processes, which have exited and await reaping. Linux `cgroups` (control groups) keep a job's processes in a tracked group so the harness can terminate them together and confirm exit before reclaiming resources [@LinuxKernel2026CgroupV2].

When process termination cannot be confirmed, the harness places the affected execution in *quarantine*. Quarantine is an enforced operational lock rather than a passive status label: the harness seals the workspace, withholds partial outputs from publication, and marks uncertain resource and license allocations as unavailable for new work. A lingering worker may still write to the old directory, but it cannot reach a retry's workspace or corrupt shared candidate artifacts. When workspace isolation and the remaining study budget permit, a retry can proceed in a fresh directory under a separate resource allocation. The quarantined attempt stays tracked until the harness confirms that its processes have exited and can safely reclaim their resources.

To bound and reclaim those allocations, the harness enforces a separate limit on each resource class an attempt can consume, including model calls, tool submissions, compute time, memory, scratch storage, and licenses. Capping process submissions does not bound a running tool's memory footprint, and killing a process does not free its commercial license seat until the license server's own release mechanism confirms that the checkout has been returned.

When the harness retries a failed run, recovery has to preserve the study's accounting history. Retrying the same design under the same tool settings keeps its `candidate_id` and `configuration_id` while creating a new execution record linked to the failed attempt. If recovery modifies any input file or tool setting, the changed configuration must receive a new configuration identifier. Each attempt retains its own outputs, measured resource use, and associated costs across compute time, memory and storage use, license occupancy, and any budgeted human repair effort. Whenever a crash or quarantine leaves a cost uncertain, the harness records that field as unknown rather than zero so that downstream methods never mistake an unfinished execution for a zero-cost evaluation.

### Categorizing Tool and Environment Failures

Keeping failed attempts distinct in the execution record also prevents a common modeling mistake: treating an infrastructure or tool failure as evidence that the candidate is a bad hardware design. A FlexLM[^fn-flexlm-c06] license checkout denial means only that the tool could not acquire a seat; a host out-of-memory failure means the cluster node lacked enough memory to finish the run. Neither event establishes that the hardware is unroutable or fails timing. If the environment records either failure as a design defect, a surrogate predictor may learn false penalties and an optimizer may discard a promising candidate that never received its intended evaluation.

Choosing the right recovery action therefore begins by separating what happened during tool execution from what the returned files say about the hardware design. @tbl-failure-taxonomy refines the five outcome classes of @sec-data-representations-world-models into nine execution conditions that the harness should keep distinct. A single run can trigger more than one condition. A node preemption may leave behind a truncated report that also causes parsing to fail, and a completed timing run may also report a setup violation, a path whose data arrives too late for its clock edge. The harness records each status attribute independently and preserves earlier successful evaluations of the candidate when a later attempt fails.

| **Recorded condition** | **How it appears** | **Preserved evidence** | **Runtime response** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Invalid request** | Illegal parameter or meaning-altering translation detected prior to invocation. | Request, validation rule, refusal reason. | Repair syntax only if meaning is preserved; otherwise refuse and return to caller. |
| **Setup / dependency failure** | Missing top-level, clock, library, constraint, or checkpoint. | Setup check, diagnostics, partial artifacts, cost. | Restore or regenerate required inputs; record which evaluation could not proceed. |
| **Infrastructure failure** | License server unreachable, host out-of-memory (OOM), scheduler preemption. | Execution record, failure source, cost, retry eligibility. | Retry if policy and resources permit; retain any partial observations and mark the interrupted evaluation incomplete. |
| **Tool failure** | Crash or tool-reported execution error, such as a gem5 crash or failed elaboration. | Tool diagnostics, exit code, partial artifacts, cost. | Inspect the diagnostic to distinguish tool malfunction, input problems, and reported design errors before choosing recovery. |
| **Incomplete return** | Missing or truncated report files. | Stage records, produced files, raw logs, parse status. | Recover retained files or regenerate missing outputs where possible; rerun only the required work. |
| **Parser failure** | An available report cannot be interpreted according to the expected schema; absent source data may also indicate an incomplete return. | Parser version, raw log, recognized tokens, residual output. | Check the report and parser version; repair parsing and reparse if the required source data is present. |
| **Formal-tool return** | SVA/BMC tool returns a proof, counterexample, bounded result, or unresolved outcome. | Original status, method, property, model, assumptions, bound, available proof or counterexample trace, cost. | Preserve the exact status and its scope, including any timeout or other reason the check remains unresolved. |
| **Reported limit violation** | Completed run reports physical violation (OpenROAD worst negative slack (WNS) $< 0$, DRC error). | Typed violation, units, conditions, raw report, cost. | Record complete return without marking run as tool failure. |
| **Complete tool return** | Expected artifacts exist and parse cleanly (including limit violations). | Typed metrics, units, conditions, warnings, raw logs, cost, lineage. | Retain return for later verification. |
: **Execution status determines what ran, not what the architecture means.** Operational failures, partial returns, parser errors, and physical violations remain separate so recovery targets exact causes. {#tbl-failure-taxonomy tbl-colwidths="[20,24,28,28]"}

Each of these conditions calls for a different next step. If a static timing tool finished cleanly but an updated report format broke the parser, fixing the parser and re-running it on the retained log recovers the result without launching another timing run. If a required cell library was missing at startup, the inputs must be repaired before the tool can answer the design question. And if a completed timing analysis reports negative slack, repeating the exact same run will only reproduce the violation; the design, constraints, or target assumptions need to change.

The same distinction applies to formal-tool returns. The harness retains native proof, counterexample, bounded, or unresolved status with the property, assumptions, and bound [@Clarke2018ModelChecking]; normalization must never turn a timeout into a pass. Timing and physical reports likewise retain their constraints and operating conditions. The verification methods in @sec-feedback-verification-trust determine what these returns support.

### Caching and Artifact Reuse

Automated hardware search faces a caching trap with two sides. Rebuilding a compiled simulator binary or a multi-hour gate-level netlist from scratch for every downstream check wastes cluster compute and commercial license seats. Yet reusing `netlist.v` simply because a file with that name sits on disk, or because it passes a `Makefile` timestamp check, can silently feed a netlist from an earlier RTL revision into an analysis of the revised candidate. Recording exact inputs, tool versions, and operating conditions lets the harness avoid both errors by reusing completed work only when its upstream dependencies match the requested operation. Under that discipline, a compiled simulator binary can serve several candidates, a synthesized gate-level netlist can feed more than one downstream analysis, and a complete raw report can be reparsed after a parser repair without launching the tool again.

To check whether those dependencies match, the harness compares evaluation keys that record the inputs and settings used to produce each artifact (including source contents, tool versions, PDK views, flags, workloads, and operating conditions), following the purely functional build discipline of identifying outputs through their complete dependency graph [@Dolstra2006Purely]. In a hardware flow, however, an omitted library corner or implicit tool default can still make two requests with matching keys evaluate different physical conditions. An evaluation key is therefore trustworthy only to the extent that its dependency list covers every input that shapes the output. A matching file hash alone never proves that a cached library view or netlist fits the requested analysis.

Artifact reuse must also remain visible in the study's accounting. Returning a cached timing report supplies an existing observation rather than a fresh, independent measurement. The new execution record must therefore point to the original producing attempt and log the near-zero lookup cost separately from the compute hours spent generating the artifact. The same rule applies to generative steps, where retained model context is also a tracked input. Reusing cached prompts or retrieved design context must follow the study's data-access and disclosure rules, so that proprietary design context never silently enters an open-source baseline run.

Reusing a completed output file is simpler than resuming execution from an intermediate checkpoint or resetting a persistent tool session. Resuming from a checkpoint continues execution from saved state, which requires the harness to verify the checkpoint's inputs, tool configuration, and execution history before building on it. A *reset*, by contrast, restores the clean starting state required by the next attempt. It initializes a fresh workspace or restores a verified baseline checkpoint, so that tool databases, emulator memory, and peripheral registers hold no leftover state. A fast soft reset that leaves memory buffers or peripheral registers populated is acceptable only when the study explicitly permits that retained state and records it.

Simply stopping a process does not reset an environment, nor does a matching checkpoint hash prove that state restoration succeeded. Whenever work runs again, its execution record states whether it started from a cold workspace or continued from retained state, preserving the resource cost of each segment without counting the same work twice. Even when reuse involves only a completed cached file, the harness must check its suitability for the requested operating conditions as well as its identity, as the stale library view illustrates.

::: {.callout-failure-mode title="The stale library view"}
**The trap.** In this illustrative failure, a design update reruns static timing analysis and receives a clean report indicating that the checked bus paths meet the requested clock period.

**The mechanism.** The analyzer loaded a cached library view that did not match the intended operating conditions. The report described checks under that stale view; it did not establish timing at the requested conditions.

**The lesson.** Checksums help identify PDK, LEF, and Liberty files; before reuse, the harness must also check that their contents suit the requested design and operating conditions.
:::

### Separating Hardware Changes from Recipe and Seed Effects {#sec-incremental-churn-dispersion}

Evaluation keys catch stale library views when inputs change within a run, but an evaluation can also go stale because the surrounding project moved on while a search was running. During an exploration campaign against a fixed baseline snapshot $t_0$, concurrent engineering work may update compiler passes, runtime software, tool versions, or RTL bus interfaces on the main branch. A candidate evaluated against snapshot $t_0$ may therefore need adaptation and re-evaluation before its results apply at $t_0 + \Delta t$.

Deciding how much work must be repeated after an upstream change is a practical bottleneck. Regenerating an entire accelerator and repeating physical synthesis after every small register or arbiter edit would make iterative search too slow for daily engineering work. To narrow what must be rerun, a harness can combine structural representations (such as CIRCT dialects, Chisel module hierarchies, and dependency-graph build tools like Bazel [@Bazel]) to identify which downstream artifacts depend on the modified sources. Syntactic module boundaries, however, tell only part of the story. An unchanged file or module boundary does not by itself prove that a cycle-level simulation result or a formal verification conclusion still holds once neighboring blocks change.

Physical implementation makes that cross-module coupling concrete. In flattened placement and routing, where one placement spans every module, a local register change inside one block can shift cell congestion, clock-tree structure, and wire routing across neighboring modules. Hierarchical floorplan partitioning, which fixes each block's region and boundary timing, can contain the work that must be repeated, provided the partition's interface, timing budgets, and physical assumptions continue to hold. The harness therefore records the basis for any artifact reuse, along with the stages repeated when upstream changes invalidate earlier assumptions. It also tracks divergence between an active search snapshot and the mainline, so the study can pause, resynchronize, or rerun affected work under a declared policy.

Shifts across design revisions are distinct from variation across repeated executions of the exact same configuration. To keep run-to-run variation interpretable, the environment must separate three mechanisms:

- **Host runtime jitter.** CPU frequency scaling, changes in memory locality, contention, and shared-storage load can alter wall-clock runtime without changing the simulated guest cycle count of a deterministic run. Execution records preserve the host placement and resource settings needed to interpret that runtime.
- **Explicit algorithmic randomness.** Generative models, stochastic search passes, and randomized EDA stages can produce different candidates, cell layouts, or timing metrics across runs. Records preserve random seeds wherever the tool exposes them, along with sampling and algorithm settings, and explicitly note when randomness controls are unavailable.
- **Parallel execution nondeterminism.** Multi-threaded tools can return different artifacts or metrics when thread counts or operating-system thread schedules change. Records preserve thread and concurrency settings rather than assuming that pinning a seed removes parallel nondeterminism.

```{python}
#| echo: false

# Recipe and seed spreads quoted below: every value is computed from the chapter
# dataset and from the retained OpenROAD placement pilot.
import csv
import re
import statistics
from pathlib import Path

import _python.plots as _ap

_root = Path(_ap.__file__).resolve().parents[2]
_recipe_csv = (
    _root / "book" / "contents" / "chapters" / "06-environments" / "data"
    / "fig-eda-runtime-variance-dispersion.csv"
)
with open(_recipe_csv, encoding="utf-8") as fh:
    _recipe_rows = list(csv.DictReader(l for l in fh if not l.startswith("#")))
_areas = {}
for _row in _recipe_rows:
    _areas.setdefault(_row["DesignName"], []).append(float(_row["ChipArea_um2"]))
assert len(_recipe_rows) == 125 and len(_areas) == 5
def _spread_pct(values):
    med = statistics.median(values)
    return 100 * (max(values) - min(values)) / med, med
def _variation_pct(values):
    return 100 * statistics.stdev(values) / statistics.mean(values)
_router_spread, _ = _spread_pct(_areas["dynamic_node"])
_gcd_spread, _gcd_median = _spread_pct(_areas["gcd"])
_other_designs = [v for k, v in _areas.items() if k != "gcd"]
_other_medians = [statistics.median(v) for v in _other_designs]
_other_variation = [_variation_pct(v) for v in _other_designs]
recipe_router_pct = f"{_router_spread:.1f}"
recipe_gcd_pct = f"{_gcd_spread:.0f}"
recipe_gcd_below_pct = f"{100 * (1 - min(_areas['gcd']) / _gcd_median):.0f}"
recipe_gcd_above_pct = f"{100 * (max(_areas['gcd']) / _gcd_median - 1):.0f}"
recipe_gcd_median_um2 = f"{_gcd_median:.1f}"
recipe_size_low = f"{min(_other_medians) / _gcd_median:.0f}"
recipe_size_high = f"{max(_other_medians) / _gcd_median:.0f}"
recipe_gcd_cv_pct = f"{_variation_pct(_areas['gcd']):.1f}"
recipe_other_cv_low = f"{min(_other_variation):.1f}"
recipe_other_cv_high = f"{max(_other_variation):.1f}"

# The only two recorded sequences with one multiset of passes in different orders.
_passes = {}
for _row in _recipe_rows:
    _key = tuple(sorted(_p.strip() for _p in _row["PassSequence"].split(";")))
    _passes.setdefault(_key, set()).add(_row["PassSequence"])
_order_pairs = [v for v in _passes.values() if len(v) > 1]
assert len(_order_pairs) == 1 and len(_order_pairs[0]) == 2
_seq_a, _seq_b = sorted(_order_pairs[0])
_by_seq = {(r["DesignName"], r["PassSequence"]): float(r["ChipArea_um2"]) for r in _recipe_rows}
_order_gap = {
    d: 100 * abs(_by_seq[(d, _seq_a)] - _by_seq[(d, _seq_b)]) / statistics.median(v)
    for d, v in _areas.items()
}
assert _order_gap["gcd"] == 0 and all(g > 0 for d, g in _order_gap.items() if d != "gcd")
order_gap_low = f"{min(g for d, g in _order_gap.items() if d != 'gcd'):.1f}"
order_gap_high = f"{max(_order_gap.values()):.1f}"

_pilot_csv = (
    _root / "data" / "studies" / "06-eda-seed-dispersion"
    / "openroad_gcd_placement_seed_pilot.csv"
)
with open(_pilot_csv, encoding="utf-8") as fh:
    _pilot = list(csv.DictReader(fh))
assert len(_pilot) == 20 and all(r["status"] == "pass" for r in _pilot)
_pilot_area = [float(r["detailedplace_instance_area_um2"]) for r in _pilot]
_pilot_wns = [float(r["detailedplace_setup_wns_ns"]) for r in _pilot]
_wns_med = statistics.median(_pilot_wns)
_wns_span = max(_pilot_wns) - min(_pilot_wns)
pilot_area_span_pct = f"{_spread_pct(_pilot_area)[0]:.2f}"
_pilot_clocks = set()
for _row in _pilot:
    _log = (_root / _row["stdout_receipt"]).read_text(encoding="utf-8", errors="replace")
    _pilot_clocks.update(re.findall(r"^Setting clock period to (\S+)$", _log, re.M))
assert len(_pilot_clocks) == 1
_clock_ns = float(_pilot_clocks.pop())
assert all(abs(w) > _clock_ns / 2 for w in _pilot_wns)
pilot_clock_ps = f"{1000 * _clock_ns:.0f}"
pilot_wns_span_period_pct = f"{100 * _wns_span / _clock_ns:.1f}"
pilot_wns_span_ps = f"{1000 * _wns_span:.1f}"
pilot_wns_median_ps = f"{1000 * _wns_med:.1f}"
```

Changing a synthesis recipe, as distinct from repeating a fixed configuration, can move mapped area with the RTL unchanged. In one retained dataset of 125 Yosys and ABC [@BraytonMishchenko2010ABC] logic-synthesis runs targeting the Nangate 45\ nm library, five open designs were each mapped under the same twenty-five ABC pass sequences (@fig-eda-runtime-variance-dispersion). Across those twenty-five sequences, the spread of mapped cell area ranged from `{python} recipe_router_pct`% of the median on an OpenPiton [@BalkindEtAl2016OpenPiton] network-on-chip (NoC) router to about `{python} recipe_gcd_pct`% (from `{python} recipe_gcd_below_pct`% below to `{python} recipe_gcd_above_pct`% above the median) on the `gcd` block, which computes a greatest common divisor. That widest span is the distance between two extreme recipes on the smallest design, which has a median area of `{python} recipe_gcd_median_um2`\ µm² while the other four are `{python} recipe_size_low` to `{python} recipe_size_high` times larger. Its coefficient of variation is `{python} recipe_gcd_cv_pct`%, against `{python} recipe_other_cv_low` to `{python} recipe_other_cv_high`% for those larger designs. Because every run used a different pass sequence, these spreads measure sensitivity to the synthesis recipe rather than run-to-run variation at a fixed recipe. They report area alone, since the flow sets no delay target and returns no timing, so a smaller mapping may simply be a slower one. Because they also compare no hardware alternatives, determining whether a recipe could hide a hardware difference requires a study that maps each candidate under matched recipes.

The original harness was not retained, but a reconstructed flow run on pinned public sources re-derives every recorded area exactly. That match still does not show that the reconstruction is the original flow, nor do the retained files record how the twenty-five sequences were chosen or whether others ran. The recorded cell and wire counts did not match Yosys output for the same flow and were removed. A sixth design whose RTL could not be identified was also removed, along with host runtime and memory columns that no retained log supports.

Explicit randomness inside a single fixed recipe leaves its own signature. In a separate pilot with pinned input sources and retained logs, twenty OpenROAD placement runs of the `gcd` example design from OpenROAD-flow-scripts on Nangate45 started from the same floorplan hash and differed only in the global-placement seed. The released records include intermediate database hashes but not the binary floorplan or placement databases themselves. Every run executed in a linux/amd64 container under ARM emulation, and a separate full-flow run on that host failed at clock-tree synthesis with an illegal instruction, so the pilot stops at placement. Across that single small design, flow stage, and host, the tool returns after detailed placement showed an area span of `{python} pilot_area_span_pct`% of its median and an estimated setup worst negative slack (WNS) span of `{python} pilot_wns_span_ps`\ ps, or `{python} pilot_wns_span_period_pct`% of the `{python} pilot_clock_ps`\ ps clock period. Every run missed that clock target by more than half a period (median WNS `{python} pilot_wns_median_ps`\ ps), so the pilot does not show how seeds behave near timing closure. Neither dataset compares hardware candidates, but both show a returned metric moving while the RTL stays fixed. It follows that an optimizer that keeps only favorable outcomes, without recording synthesis recipes and random seeds, leaves downstream analysis unable to separate an architectural improvement from a fortunate tool setting or seed.[^fn-lucky-seed-c06]

[^fn-lucky-seed-c06]: **Seed and recipe sensitivity**: Match recipes across candidates and repeat stochastic evaluations to assess uncertainty in the candidate differences. The raw spread of outcomes is not a universal threshold for resolving an improvement. Claims that should hold across recipes also require comparisons under the relevant recipes.

![**Unchanged RTL can return a different mapped area under a different synthesis recipe.** Relative cell-area deviation from each design's median across 25 ABC pass sequences in Yosys on the Nangate 45\ nm library (125 runs across five open designs, with areas re-derived from pinned sources by a reconstructed flow). Spreads range from `{python} recipe_router_pct`% on the OpenPiton router to about `{python} recipe_gcd_pct`% on the GCD block, the smallest design.](images/fig-eda-runtime-variance-dispersion.png){#fig-eda-runtime-variance-dispersion width="100%" fig-alt="Box plot with overlaid points of 125 logic synthesis runs across five open hardware designs, showing mapped area as a percentage deviation from each design median. The PicoRV32 core, NoC router, AES-128, and SHA-256 designs show narrow spreads and the GCD block shows the widest spread, and each design is drawn with its own marker shape."}

These distributions show that the mapped area from a deterministic flow is one point in a recipe-dependent range. Logic-optimization passes such as rewriting, refactoring, and balancing are heuristics applied in sequence [@BraytonMishchenko2010ABC], each working on the network its predecessor left, so both the choice of passes and their order can change the result. Two of the twenty-five recorded sequences hold the same passes in different orders, and their areas differ by `{python} order_gap_low`% to `{python} order_gap_high`% of the median on four designs and match exactly on `gcd`. One pair shows that order can matter on these designs, not how much it usually does. Repeating a fixed recipe would expose none of this, because the reconstructed flow returns the same area for a given recipe. A credible study therefore has to record and match exact recipes, repeat the stages that are stochastic with their seeds recorded, and log resource consumption alongside quality-of-results metrics. Downstream statistical methods then test whether an observed gain reflects an architectural improvement or a recipe or seed effect (@sec-feedback-verification-trust). The environment's job is to capture the complete execution records that make that test possible.

## Execution Records {#sec-execution-records}

When a harness returns only a bare dictionary of scalar metrics to the search loop, operational failures masquerade as hardware properties: an unparsed power report defaults to `0.0`, an in-place retry overwrites the license-hours burned by earlier crashes, and a single setup-slack number hides hold-time violations or unmeasured operating corners. To preserve the full context around those numbers, the execution record introduced in @sec-architecture-20-ontology becomes an explicit runtime schema that answers what work was attempted, what happened during execution, and what can be examined afterward. Because one record is created per tool attempt across the execution lifecycle, a refused request logs why no tool ran, an attempt spanning several backend jobs links their outcomes together, and a later retry adds to the candidate's history rather than overwriting the failed attempt.

Six groups of information make the record complete:

- **Request and attempt identity:** Study, request, run specification, candidate, configuration, workload, attempt universally unique identifier, submission token, and attached scheduler job identifiers.
- **Starting state:** Input artifacts, source revisions, tool and container versions, library views, and operating conditions.
- **Execution outcome:** Admission status, job outcomes, terminal cause, artifact completeness, parser status, and recovery eligibility.
- **Returned material:** Raw reports and logs, artifact references and hashes, structured metrics with units and scope, warnings, and unrecognized output.
- **Lineage and retries:** Dependencies, producing transformations, and links to earlier attempts or restored checkpoints, with references to any checks performed.
- **Resource use and cost:** Wall-clock time, CPU/accelerator hours, peak memory, storage use, license-hours, and charges, distinguishing measured values from estimates or unknowns.

An unavailable measurement states its absence and cause, distinguishing an unmeasured property from a parser failure or an inapplicable field. A timing summary, for example, must link to the checked paths, corners, and constraints rather than presenting one slack value as the state of the whole design. Those links let later verification inspect the completed checks, while the recorded resource use supports comparison of the effort spent obtaining them.

How much a record must hold depends on the claim it supports. Manual drafting often relies on developer notes, terminal logs, and version-control commits, while a harness can track parameter vectors, simulator seeds, and costs for automated sweeps. For a study that makes an implementation or signoff claim, the record must link the high-level intent and intermediate compiler representations to the netlists, physical-design artifacts, and reports supporting that claim. These records document which checks ran and what they returned; they do not by themselves certify physical viability.

```{python}
#| echo: false
import csv as _csv6sc
import json as _json6sc
from pathlib import Path as _Path6sc
import _python.plots as _ap6sc

_sc20_dir = _Path6sc(_ap6sc.__file__).resolve().parents[2] / "data" / "studies" / "20-implementation-stage-costs"
_sc20_bounds = _json6sc.loads((_sc20_dir / "time_boundaries.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
_sc20_rows = list(_csv6sc.DictReader((_sc20_dir / "stage-costs.csv").open(encoding="utf-8")))
