```{python}
_sc20_top = max(_sc20_rows, key=lambda r: float(r["runtime_seconds"]))
sc20_steps_n = len(_sc20_rows)
sc20_sum_s = f"{_sc20_bounds['sum_step_intervals_seconds']:.1f}"
sc20_test_s = f"{_sc20_bounds['run_test_job_step_seconds']:.0f}"
sc20_job_s = f"{_sc20_bounds['complete_design_job_seconds']:.0f}"
sc20_route_s = f"{float(_sc20_top['runtime_seconds']):.2f}"
sc20_job_over_steps = f"{_sc20_bounds['complete_design_job_seconds'] / _sc20_bounds['sum_step_intervals_seconds']:.1f}"
```

Complete records also support later efforts to reproduce the work. The Association for Computing Machinery artifact review guidelines distinguish *repeatability* (same team, same setup), *reproducibility* (different team, same setup), and *replicability* (different team, different setup) [@ACM2020ArtifactReview], and the Popper convention similarly emphasizes preserving executable evaluation workflows [@JimenezEtAl2017PopperConvention]. An execution record supplies the metadata needed for these activities, though carrying them out still requires access to the underlying artifacts and a runnable procedure. Even with identical recorded inputs, host runtime or returned metrics can vary for the reasons examined in @sec-incremental-churn-dispersion. Wall-clock cost also depends on whether the record measures individual flow steps or the enclosing job (@fig-ch06-implementation-stage-costs).

![**Recorded runtime depends on which execution boundary the harness measures.** (a) Individual flow steps in one LibreLane implementation run of the `spm` design on the IHP SG13G2 130\ nm BiCMOS PDK [@LibreLane2026SpmSg13g2Run; @IHPOpenPDK], where `{python} sc20_steps_n` outer steps total `{python} sc20_sum_s`\ s and OpenROAD detailed routing takes `{python} sc20_route_s`\ s. (b) Three nested boundaries for the same run: summed steps (`{python} sc20_sum_s`\ s), the `Run Test` job step (`{python} sc20_test_s`\ s), and the full continuous-integration job (`{python} sc20_job_s`\ s).](images/fig-ch06-implementation-stage-costs){#fig-ch06-implementation-stage-costs width="100%" fig-alt="Two-panel horizontal bar chart of recorded execution times from a single LibreLane physical-implementation run on the IHP SG13G2 PDK. Panel (a) shows the six longest individual flow steps, led by OpenROAD detailed routing, alongside the combined remainder of the steps. Panel (b) compares three nested accounting boundaries, each longer than the last: the sum of step intervals, the Run Test job step, and the complete CI job."}

In this LibreLane run, the `{python} sc20_steps_n` outer flow steps, led by OpenROAD detailed routing and followed by Magic LEF generation and streamout and then KLayout and Magic DRC, total `{python} sc20_sum_s`\ s. The enclosing `Run Test` job step takes `{python} sc20_test_s`\ s; runner preparation, repository checkout, Nix store and PDK cache restores, and artifact upload bring the full continuous-integration job to `{python} sc20_job_s`\ s, or `{python} sc20_job_over_steps` times the summed steps. These intervals nest rather than add, so runtime comparisons must name their accounting boundary. One run selected from a development branch can show that these boundaries differ, but not what a physical-design flow typically costs.

## Mobile XR Subsystem Evaluation Environment {#sec-mobile-xr-evaluation}

The prospective Lighthouse cache study provides a compact example of how an environment turns a study plan into conditional tool execution. It compares 2\ MiB, 3\ MiB, and 4\ MiB cache capacities while holding the surrounding compute organization, software stack, and workload fixed. Extending the mobile XR baseline from @sec-moonshot, the illustrative subsystem sketched earlier in this chapter pairs an NPU ($16 \times 16$ array) and dual LPDDR5 channels under a 3\ W power budget in a 3\ nm-class process such as TSMC N3E. These choices describe one prospective study plan rather than a completed Lighthouse implementation.

The intended target comparison remains unexecuted because its capacity-to-hardware construction rule, tool inputs, and measurement procedures are not yet fully specified. The prospective plan in @tbl-environment-contract adds a screening rule to the design-loop card of @sec-architecture-20-ontology: a candidate must clear area and access-time screening before consuming a cycle-level attempt. The four-attempt budget includes recovery and repeated runs, so a screened-out candidate leaves its planned attempt available for other work. After the plan, a retained analytical run at a different supported process node demonstrates why a tool can finish without answering the requested question. A hypothetical continuation then applies the plan under assumed technology support.

| **Run category** | **Prospective XR subsystem evaluation plan** |
| --- | --- |
| **Candidates and fixed state** | Vary only `l2.capacity` among 2\ MiB, 3\ MiB, and 4\ MiB. Hold the NPU organization, RISC-V cores, memory arbitration, NoC, software binary, XR workload, and cache policies fixed. A specified rule must derive each legal SRAM organization from capacity; capacity alone does not identify its banks, geometry, or macro composition. |
| **Translation and identity** | Prepare SRAM-model inputs and a compatible cycle-level path. Preserve candidate, workload, tool, library, and operating-condition identities. Power estimates require an identified model and activity inputs; another tool path requires its own supported representations. |
| **Order and dispatch** | Once prerequisites are bound, perform analytical screening. Admit cycle-level work only when the screening return is complete, matches its schema, and reports area $\le 1.5\text{ mm}^2$ and access time $\le 2.5\text{ ns}$. Passing this screening check permits further evaluation; it does not establish candidate superiority. |
| **Matched work and limits** | Use matched workload and operating conditions for baseline and alternatives. Budget three screening runs and at most four cycle-level attempts, including recovery attempts. Apply specified queue, execution, and study deadlines. RTL synthesis and physical signoff are outside this exploratory budget. |
| **Failures and recovery** | Keep infrastructure failures, tool errors, incomplete returns, and parser failures distinct. Reparse retained material when sufficient; when execution must be retried, create a linked attempt from the required starting state and charge it to the budget. |
| **Containment and reuse** | Restrict each attempt's access to tools and writable paths. Quarantine unconfirmed terminations. Reuse artifacts only when their dependencies and conditions match the intended operation, preserving links to the producing attempts. |
| **Returns, cost, and lineage** | Retain SRAM area, access time, energy and leakage estimates; frame records, memory traffic, and subsystem power with their modeling assumptions. Link those values to raw reports, warnings, input artifacts, and attempt costs. |
| **Decisions left outside** | The harness enforces the supplied dispatch and stopping rules. The method or architect determines measurement validity, comparative conclusions, and whether to advance a candidate or revise the study. |
: **An environment executes the study's rules while retaining their inputs and consequences.** This prospective plan separates preparation, conditional dispatch, recovery, and interpretation; it is not a completed execution specification. {#tbl-environment-contract tbl-colwidths="[24,76]"}

```{python}
#| echo: false
# Retained 22 nm returns for the three Lighthouse capacities: CACTI 7 output written by
# data/run_cacti_lighthouse_l2.py and data/run_cacti_lighthouse_l2_lop.py from
# data/cacti_lighthouse_l2.cfg.in. They cannot screen the 3 nm-class target.
_cacti_csv = (
    _root / "book" / "contents" / "chapters" / "06-environments" / "data"
    / "cacti-lighthouse-l2.csv"
)
with open(_cacti_csv, encoding="utf-8") as fh:
    _cacti = {
        (r["device_type"], int(r["capacity_mib"])): r
        for r in csv.DictReader(l for l in fh if not l.startswith("#"))
    }
assert len(_cacti) == 6
with open(_cacti_csv.with_name("cacti-lighthouse-l2-lop.csv"), encoding="utf-8") as fh:
    _cacti.update(
        ((r["device_type"], int(r["capacity_mib"])), r)
        for r in csv.DictReader(l for l in fh if not l.startswith("#"))
    )
assert len(_cacti) == 9


def _cv(device, mib, col):
    return float(_cacti[(device, mib)][col])


_mibs = (2, 3, 4)
hp_area = [f"{_cv('itrs-hp', m, 'area_mm2'):.1f}" for m in _mibs]
hp_acc = [f"{_cv('itrs-hp', m, 'access_time_ns'):.1f}" for m in _mibs]
lp_acc = [f"{_cv('itrs-lstp', m, 'access_time_ns'):.1f}" for m in _mibs]
lop_acc = [f"{_cv('itrs-lop', m, 'access_time_ns'):.1f}" for m in _mibs]
assert all(_cv("itrs-hp", m, "area_mm2") > 1.5 for m in _mibs)
assert all(_cv("itrs-lstp", m, "area_mm2") > 1.5 for m in _mibs)
assert all(_cv("itrs-lop", m, "area_mm2") > 1.5 for m in _mibs)
assert all(_cv("itrs-hp", m, "access_time_ns") <= 2.5 for m in _mibs)
assert all(_cv("itrs-lstp", m, "access_time_ns") > 2.5 for m in _mibs)
assert all(_cv("itrs-lop", m, "access_time_ns") > 2.5 for m in _mibs)
```

The retained analytical run uses CACTI 7 [@BalasubramonianEtAl2017CACTI7]. The pinned version supports technology nodes only down to 22\ nm (a retained probe shows it rejecting 21, 20, 16, and 3\ nm), so it cannot evaluate the 3\ nm-class Lighthouse target. A retained run instead evaluates the 2, 3, and 4\ MiB capacities at 22\ nm with 64-byte lines, 16 ways, and one bank. CACTI chooses the internal array organizations under its energy-delay-squared objective. High-performance devices return areas of `{python} hp_area[0]`, `{python} hp_area[1]`, and `{python} hp_area[2]`\ mm², all above the target study's $1.5\text{ mm}^2$ limit. Their access times range from `{python} hp_acc[0]` to `{python} hp_acc[2]`\ ns and fall below the 2.5\ ns limit; low-operating-power devices instead return `{python} lop_acc[0]` to `{python} lop_acc[2]`\ ns and low-standby-power devices `{python} lp_acc[0]` to `{python} lp_acc[2]`\ ns, which exceed it. Those two device types also exceed the area limit at all three capacities. The configuration, script, raw tool output, and parsed returns are retained with the chapter data.

Those are actual model returns for a different process. Applying the target thresholds to them cannot accept or reject the 3\ nm candidates. An environment enforcing the stated dispatch rule must report the node mismatch and wait for a suitable model, rather than silently substituting 22\ nm for the requested process. The architect could authorize a separate performance-only study under explicit memory assumptions, as discussed in @sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization, while leaving physical feasibility unresolved. That would change the study plan, not repair the missing technology support.

Suppose such a 3\ nm model were available and admitted the 2\ MiB and 3\ MiB candidates while rejecting the 4\ MiB candidate above an area or latency limit. Under this plan, the 4\ MiB candidate would receive no cycle-level dispatch. Its screening record would remain on file for review, though failing an analytical screen would not by itself prove physical infeasibility.

A hypothetical execution sequence might then spend the four-attempt cycle-level budget as follows:

1. The 2\ MiB baseline completes a cycle-level evaluation.
2. The 3\ MiB attempt encounters a setup failure and returns no usable cycle-level result.
3. After the setup problem is repaired, a linked retry of the same 3\ MiB candidate completes under the intended conditions.
4. A planned repeat of the 3\ MiB evaluation consumes the final attempt.

Inspecting the execution records afterward shows four attempts charged to the budget, but only three completed cycle-level evaluations. The failed attempt preserves its setup diagnostics and consumed cost, and the recovery retry remains distinct from the planned repeat. This four-step trace illustrates honest accounting rather than a sufficient statistical comparison; the search method or architect still has to judge whether three completed runs support a design decision. What the environment provides is an auditable record of what was admitted, what ran, what returned, and what remained unresolved. Scaling that isolation and provenance discipline across closed-source tools and large chip hierarchies raises several open research questions.

## Open Questions

Building isolated tool harnesses and keeping complete execution records exposes four open problems in how we run and audit hardware design tools:

- **How can we verify which checks a closed-source EDA tool actually ran without repeating the entire analysis?** An exit code of zero and a cleanly formatted report from a closed-source synthesis or static timing engine do not by themselves confirm that the tool applied the requested operating corner, used the intended wire-load model, or checked the paths an inherited constraint waiver may have excluded. Parsing text logs catches only the omissions a vendor binary chooses to print, yet rerunning the full analysis in a second reference tool gives up the speed the harness was built to provide. We still lack lightweight canary checks, input-perturbation probes, or execution-trace attestations that can confirm an opaque tool exercised the requested corners and constraints. Such checks would keep the runtime question of whether the requested check ran separate from the modeling question of whether that check adequately captures physical effects such as voltage droop.[^fn-voltage-droop-c06]

[^fn-voltage-droop-c06]: **Voltage droop**: A temporary decrease in supply voltage, which can occur when switching activity changes the current drawn from the power delivery network. It can change cell delays; assessing its timing consequences requires voltage assumptions or analyses that cover the relevant variation.

- **When we reuse a running hardware emulator or persistent EDA session across candidates, how do we guarantee that no state leaks from one run to the next?** Reinitializing an FPGA emulation cluster from a cold bitstream reload or rebuilding an in-memory physical-design database from scratch for every candidate can take longer than the evaluation itself. Warm resets and checkpoint continuations avoid that setup penalty, but they risk leaving residual state in external DRAM buffers, unmapped peripheral registers, or cached parasitic timing graphs that silently contaminates the next candidate's measurement. We still need restoration methods that cover all state relevant to the next evaluation and checks that expose any gaps in that coverage, at lower setup cost than full reinitialization.

- **When an engineer or generator edits one hardware module, how do we know which cached layout and timing results elsewhere on the chip remain valid?** Content-addressed build systems track syntactic file dependencies cleanly, but physical chip implementation couples neighboring modules together. In flattened placement and routing, modifying a single arbiter or register stage can shift macro congestion, wire parasitics, and clock-tree skew across adjacent blocks whose source RTL never changed. Rerunning full-chip synthesis and place-and-route after every minor upstream edit makes continuous co-design too slow for daily work, whereas trusting module-level file hashes alone lets stale timing and power numbers slip through. We still lack reliable ways to combine intermediate compiler representations (such as CIRCT) with physical floorplan partitions and interface slack margins to prove when a local change stays contained within a region. With such proof, a harness could limit incremental re-evaluation to the places where physical coupling invalidates earlier execution records.

- **How can we tell a genuine architectural improvement from a lucky synthesis recipe or placement seed without multiplying our compute and license budgets?** In @sec-incremental-churn-dispersion, changing the logic-optimization recipe on unchanged RTL moved mapped area, and changing the placement seed on one small design moved placed area and estimated setup slack. An architectural effect of similar size could disappear inside those spreads unless a study compares candidates under matched recipes and repeated seeds. Running a full matrix of recipes and random seeds for every proposed candidate would quickly exhaust cluster compute and commercial EDA license seats, whereas evaluating a single seed invites an optimizer to mistake a fortunate tool run for a better microarchitecture. We still need adaptive scheduling policies that allocate repeated runs and recipe comparisons where uncertainty or recipe sensitivity could change candidate selection, matching the evidence to the scope of the study's claims within its compute and license budgets.

## Summary

An execution environment connects design methods to the simulators, compilers, formal engines, and physical-design flows that construct and evaluate hardware candidates. During setup, the environment defines the actions a method may request (including whether it can submit new RTL or only adjust parameters inside a fixed template) and establishes the tool paths and lineage rules that identify every input. At runtime, the harness schedules work across cluster nodes and license pools, isolates faults, and records the history of each attempt. Returned observations then carry enough context to show what each result actually describes.

::: {.callout-takeaways}
- **Interfaces define the available design actions.** Specify what a method may inspect, submit, change, and evaluate. Wrappers translate those requests into tool inputs and return structured results without silently changing the candidate or its conditions.
- **Tool choice follows the property being evaluated.** Behavioral checks, timing models, formal analyses, and physical implementation answer different questions. Preserve each path's assumptions, scope, and units when combining their outputs. Include the physical and formal checks needed for the properties the study claims.
- **Every execution attempt needs its own record.** Link requests to backend jobs, outputs, failures, and costs. Distinguish duplicate submissions from deliberate retries, enforce admission limits so proposals do not overwhelm evaluation capacity, and keep raw reports, warnings, and missing values beside the parsed metrics.
- **Recovery and reuse require controlled state.** Isolate writable workspaces, respect data-access restrictions, confirm termination, and manage shared licenses. Reuse an artifact or checkpoint only when it applies to the requested operation; a matching identifier alone is insufficient.
- **Repeated execution is part of the evaluation plan.** Budget for variation, retain recipes, seeds, and settings, and distinguish randomness from host interference and parallel nondeterminism. A cached result is an existing observation, not a new repeat.
:::

Recording what ran and what returned is the foundation for closing the design loop, but an execution record does not interpret itself. To decide what those observations prove and how they should steer the search, the design loop must connect verification, statistical feedback, and learning to the next design choice (@sec-feedback-verification-trust).
